angola.description: The oldest and most fundamental toque of Capoeira Angola. A slow, deep rhythm, played on the berimbau gunga, that sets the philosophical, cautious tone of the *jogo*.
angola.context: Played at the start of every Angola game. It sets up a game close to the ground, full of *malícia* and contemplation. The most senior mestre plays the gunga and leads the *roda*.
angola.gameCharacter: Slow, low to the ground, cunning, philosophical

sao-bento-pequeno.description: Also called 'Inverted Angola.' The gunga's high and low notes are swapped, creating a subtle variation that signals a close, careful game.
sao-bento-pequeno.context: A close, tight game requiring great attention. The capoeiristas stay near each other, reading every small movement the opponent makes.

sao-bento-grande-angola.description: A fast, expansive rhythm within Capoeira Angola. It allows for wide, acrobatic movement while keeping the essence of Angola-style *mandinga*.
sao-bento-grande-angola.context: Played for more open, faster games within the Angola tradition. It widens the playing space without losing the Angola philosophy.

sao-bento-grande-regional.description: Created by Mestre Bimba for Capoeira Regional. An explosive, fast, sharply marked rhythm that drives a dynamic game of direct strikes and quick dodges.
sao-bento-grande-regional.context: The main toque of Capoeira Regional. It sets up a fast, athletic game played at a greater distance. It's also widely used in Capoeira Contemporânea and Abadá *rodas*.
sao-bento-grande-regional.gameCharacter: Explosive, athletic, wide distance, direct strikes

iuna.description: A medium-tempo toque, graceful and elegant. In Capoeira Regional it is played exclusively for graduates and mestres.
iuna.context: Reserved for graduated players in Regional *rodas*. It calls for technical and philosophical maturity. In Abadá it may be played at special moments such as *batizados*.
iuna.gameCharacter: Graceful, elegant, technical, reserved for graduates

santa-maria.description: One of the toques from Mestre Bimba's original sequence. A striking, solemn rhythm associated with a game of precision and mutual respect.
santa-maria.context: Played in formal training settings and Capoeira Regional events. It encourages a technical game of well-defined movement without excess.

idalina.description: A soft, delicate toque from the Regional repertoire. The name is feminine, and the toque reflects that elegance — it invites a game of fluid movement and expressiveness.
idalina.context: Played for demonstration games and lighter moments in the *roda*. It values creativity and bodily expressiveness over power.

amazonas.description: A dynamic toque from Mestre Bimba's repertoire, evoking the vastness and power of the Amazon rainforest. Its rhythm swings between tension and lightness.
amazonas.context: It encourages a game of great range, with wide movement and creative use of space. Capoeiristas explore acrobatics and takedowns fluidly.

cavalaria.description: A toque historically used to warn capoeiristas that the mounted police were arriving, from the period when capoeira was outlawed in Brazil (before 1937).
cavalaria.context: When Cavalaria sounded, capoeiristas would stop the game and pretend to be working. Today it is played at special events and for educational purposes, recalling capoeira's history of resistance.
cavalaria.gameCharacter: Historic, alerting, a signal of danger

sao-bento-abada.description: The main toque of Abadá-Capoeira, developed within the tradition founded by Mestre Camisa. It combines the energy of São Bento Regional with Abadá's own identity.
sao-bento-abada.context: Played in Abadá-Capoeira *rodas* and *batizados*. It sets the base rhythm of the game in the school's tradition, encouraging speed, power, and technical precision.

benguela.description: A slow, fluid toque from the Abadá tradition. It invites the 'jogo de floreios' — a beautiful, cooperative game full of bodily expressiveness.
benguela.context: It encourages a game close to the ground, cooperative and aesthetically beautiful. Capoeiristas show off flourishes, balance, and creativity. It isn't a fighting game but a bodily dialogue.
benguela.gameCharacter: Fluid, cooperative, beautiful, expressive, close to the ground

siriunha.description: A vibrant toque of Abadá-Capoeira, also spelled Siriúna. An upbeat rhythm that energizes the *roda* and invites an agile, joyful game.
siriunha.context: Played to liven up high-spirited moments in the Abadá *roda*. Capoeiristas respond with livelier movement, acrobatics, and playful interaction.

jogo-dos-bichos.description: A playful, distinctive toque of Abadá-Capoeira. Capoeiristas imitate the movements of animals — cat, monkey, snake, alligator — turning the game into a theater of bodily expression.
jogo-dos-bichos.context: Especially popular in children's classes and cultural performances. It builds creativity, body awareness, and a connection to nature. Each animal has its own movement pattern.

capuxadama.description: A distinctive toque of Abadá-Capoeira with a striking rhythm and identity all its own. Little known outside the Abadá tradition, it is part of the repertoire taught to graduates.
capuxadama.context: Played within Abadá's own settings, such as graduation events and regional gatherings. It reinforces the school's identity and community ties.

toque-do-berimbau.description: A reverential toque of Abadá-Capoeira that celebrates the berimbau itself and its central role in capoeira. A contemplative rhythm inviting reflection on musicality.
toque-do-berimbau.context: Played to honor the berimbau at special moments in the Abadá *roda*. Capoeiristas pause to listen and take in the musicality before resuming the game.

capopasso.description: A dynamic toque of Abadá-Capoeira with a distinctive rhythmic character. It is part of the musical vocabulary taught within the tradition founded by Mestre Camisa.
capopasso.context: Present in Abadá's internal *rodas* and in musical training curricula. It develops musicians' skill and players' bodily response to the rhythm.
capopasso.gameCharacter: Dynamic, sharply marked, instructive, distinctly Abadá

samba-de-roda.description: The rhythm of the traditional Sambas de Roda from the Recôncavo Baiano region, considered one of Brazil's oldest rhythms. In capoeira it is played on the berimbau viola as a celebration after the *roda*.
samba-de-roda.context: Played at the end of Angola *rodas* to celebrate. Capoeiristas and musicians sing and dance samba de roda around the *bateria* (the music section). It can also appear in cultural performances.

maculele.description: The rhythm of the Maculelê warrior dance, originating in Santo Amaro da Purificação, Bahia. Dancers strike sticks (biriba wood batons) or machetes together in time with the music.
maculele.context: Played during Maculelê performances — the warriors' stick dance. It is often presented at *batizados* and Abadá cultural events alongside capoeira.
maculele.gameCharacter: Warrior-like, percussive, theatrical, sharply marked rhythm

paranue-paranua.notes: One of the oldest and best-known *ladainhas*. The word 'Paranauê' has no direct translation — it's a calling or invocation cry, possibly of Yoruba origin.

zum-zum-zum.notes: 'Me matou' ('killed me') here means 'completely won me over' — a metaphorical death from a passion for capoeira. The 'Zum Zum Zum' imitates the sound of the berimbau.

vou-lhe-dizer-o-que-me-alegra.notes: The 'Hino do Abadá' ('Anthem of Abadá', also known as 'Vou lhe dizer o que me alegra') is the signature song of the ABADÁ-Capoeira association, composed by Lampréia and Macaco Preto. The lyrics express the joy and energy of a capoeira *roda* with the full *bateria* and the sound of the berimbau.
